recorded.rule: Q2 v2: a giveaway, read from the question's own text alone
recorded.prompt:q-reference: Answer ONLY from this question's own text: its stem and its options. Use no knowledge of the subject at all; treat every term as a word you have never met. Pick an option only when the wording itself singles it out: it is longer or more specific than the others, it repeats words from the stem, the others carry absolute terms such as 'always' or 'never', the stem's grammar fits it alone, or it restates the stem. A cue decides only when it clearly singles out one option over every other; a weak cue, or one another option shares, decides nothing. Otherwise answer 'none'. Say which cue decided it, or that none did.

recorded.prompt:q-reference:a: Read the page and each keyed question. For every wrong option, say whether a passage of the page rules it out, and quote or name that passage.
recorded.pass:q-reference:a: an independent reader (21-synchronization q3), never the author
recorded.outcome:q-reference:a: ruled out: "Assuming `volatile` on a reference makes the object's fields visible": "volatile Config config; // Only the reference 'config' is volatile" / "config.value is NOT automatically volatile!" — directly contradicts 'each field of its object' becoming volatile.
recorded.prompt:q-reference:b: Read the page and each keyed question. For every wrong option, say whether a passage of the page rules it out, and quote or name that passage.
recorded.pass:q-reference:b: an independent reader (21-synchronization q3), never the author
recorded.outcome:q-reference:b: ruled out: The page's own example uses this exact code and states: "config.value = newValue; // Not ordered by any volatile write: other threads may not see it" — it does not say the field is merely flushed later at the next read of the reference; it says there is no ordering guarantee at all, so other threads may never see it.
recorded.prompt:q-history:a: Read the page and each keyed question. For every wrong option, say whether a passage of the page rules it out, and quote or name that passage.
recorded.pass:q-history:a: an independent reader (21-synchronization q3), never the author
recorded.outcome:q-history:a: ruled out: Evolution Across Java Versions: 'Java 1.0–1.4: volatile accesses were ordered among themselves, but ordinary reads and writes could be reordered around them, so a volatile write could not publish other data.' The page says volatile accesses were ordered among themselves (not reordered with each other); the reordering problem was with ordinary accesses around volatile ones.
recorded.prompt:q-history:c: Read the page and each keyed question. For every wrong option, say whether a passage of the page rules it out, and quote or name that passage.
recorded.pass:q-history:c: an independent reader (21-synchronization q3), never the author
recorded.outcome:q-history:c: ruled out: The page attributes the pre-Java-5 breakage specifically to reordering, not tearing: Q3's answer says 'Before Java 5 (JSR 133) it was broken even with volatile, because volatile did not order the constructor's ordinary writes,' and the Evolution section says the cause was that 'ordinary reads and writes could be reordered around them.' Separately, Q2 states without any version qualifier that 'volatile IS atomic for: Single reads and writes of any type (including long and double)' and the Edge Cases section attributes 64-bit tearing only to non-volatile long/double ('Reads/writes to 64-bit non-volatile long and double may not be atomic... volatile makes them atomic'), never to volatile reference reads/writes.
